newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: RAAF PLANES ON STAND-BY FOR CAMBODIA EVACUATION
Federal Defence Minister, Ian McLachlan, says no decision has been made on whether to send RAAF aircraft to pick up Australians in Cambodia.
Two C-130 transport aircraft have been sent to Butterworth Airfield in Malaysia to stand-by for any emergency evacuations.
But Mr McLachlan says he hopes the transport planes will not have to be sent any further than Malaysia.
He says it "seems as though things have calmed down a little bit in Cambodia".
But Mr McLachlan says Australian citizens still may require airlifting, if the situation deteriorates.
He says Australian troops will accompany the RAAF aircraft if they are required.
The first C-130 is due to arrive at Butterworth at 12.30 a.m. tomorrow, with the second aircraft three hours behind it.
The Defence Department says the aircraft, flying from Victoria's Richmond air base, are carrying troops, aero-medical evacuation staff, and extra flight crew.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister John Howard says as well as the 517 Australians in Cambodia, a number of Canadians will also be looked after.
CALL FOR AUSTRALIA, OTHERS, TO INTERVENE IN CAMBODIA
The former head of the Foreign Affairs Department, Michael Costello, says Australia and other parties to the Paris Peace Accords should urgently intervene in the crisis in Cambodia.
Mr Costello was involved in negotiating the political solution which led to the Paris Peace Accords, and UN supervised elections, in Cambodia in 1993.
He says Cambodia's two Prime Ministers, Hun Sen and Prince Norodom Ranariddh, would have had no choice but to listen to other countries because Cambodia's future depends on foriegn aid and support.
Mr Costello says the west should be deeply concerned about the human rights issues involved.

He says: "The Paris Peace Accords give us a standing and status under those accords, and we should, in my view, be urgently trying to get together the parties to those accords now to try as a group to go forward..."
Mr Costello says such action should not be taken just by individual countries, but by all nations involved in the framing of the accords.
Besides Australia, these countries include the United States, Japan, and Cambodia's neighbours.
HUNTER COAL STRIKE FOCUS FOR GOVT, UNIONS

Federal Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, has warned unions considering secondary boycotts in support of the miners' union Hunter Valley strike, of laws against such action. The CFMEU has solidarity agreements with the Transport Workers' and Maritime Unions, and it is thought they will be enacted if coal from the Hunter Valley Number One mine, in New South Wales, is shipped today.
Mr Reith says workers away from the mine should be simply concerned about their own company's position, "rather than trying to fight for someone else's terms and conditions and negotiations...".
He says the other unions would be aware of the legal provisions in place to prevent secondary boycotts, and has appealed to them to take a sensible, rather than ideological, approach.
Meanwhile, ACTU President, Jennie George, has told strikers at the mine they should stand firm and fight for their rights.
Ms George told workers they are being used as a test case by the Federal Government.
And the Mineworkers' union says the owners of the mine should not bother to send more trains to the site, which has been picketed by the union for the past month.
Rio Tinto is expected to try to get a train through the picket line shortly, despite the failure of a similar attempt last week.
OPPOSITION KEEPS UP PROSSER PRESSURE
The Federal Opposition says it is a disgrace the Prime Minister has not even contacted Small Business Minister, Geoff Prosser, since returning to Australia.

The Opposition says it is a damning indictment of Mr Howard's approach to ministerial standards that he has been back five days, but has not even telephoned Mr Prosser to discuss his business activities.
Labor's continuing to call for Mr Prosser's resignation or sacking on the grounds his private business interests conflict with his ministerial duties.

Shadow Small Business Minister, Stephen Martin, says he has arranged to send Mr Howard copies of newspaper articles, parliamentary transcripts and records of interview, relating to Mr Prosser's business dealings.
He has urged the Prime Minister to flick through them while he watches the cricket on television.
CROWN CASINO LAYING OFF CASUALS
Crown Casino says a majority of redundancies at its Southbank complex will involve casual staff and people hired specifically to help establish its permanent venue.
Crown says it hired a large number of casual and agency staff, from security to recruitment people, to help in the pre-opening and opening phase.
The casino says some positions are no longer needed.
Crown Chairman, Lloyd Williams, dismissed newspaper reports that up to 500 jobs would be lost, saying the figure was around 40.
The Casino has since put out a statement, saying it is now recruiting an additional 250 staff.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
